facts.text: Timberlane began as agricultural land in the early 1900s, part of Jefferson Parish’s West Bank expansion near New Orleans.
The Harvey Canal locks, finished in 1907, joined the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway in 1924, boosting drainage and shipping for Timberlane’s farms.
After World War II, the GI Bill enabled veterans to buy homes, sparking a boom that turned Timberlane’s former pecan groves into ranch‑style suburbs.
In 1959, Timberlane Estates opened as a golf‑course community, the West Bank’s first private country club designed by Robert Trent Jones.
Timberlane sits on the West Bank of the Mississippi River, just south of the river near Marrero, linking it to New Orleans.
Early Timberlane land supported low‑intensity farming—truck crops, pecan orchards, cattle grazing, and forestry—while sharecropping linked local African American workers to the area.
